explanation: The passive is present simple (“are preserved”), so the active should also be present simple: “preserves.” Hence (a) is correct. (b) changes aspect to present perfect; (c) changes tense to past; (d) changes to present continuous. Learning points: match tense when changing voice; passive present simple = am/is/are + V3; active present simple = base verb with -s/-es for singular subject; “by + agent” becomes the subject in active; keep purpose phrases (“for future generations”) unchanged.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?

Why weren’t the authorities intimated about the theft?
options: Why didn’t they intimate the authorities about the theft?
Why haven’t they intimated the authorities about the theft?
Why don’t they intimate the authorities about the theft?
Why hasn’t anyone intimated the authorities about the theft?
explanation: The passive is simple past negative interrogative (“weren’t intimated”), so the active should be simple past negative interrogative: “didn’t … intimate.” Option (a) fits. (b) is present perfect; (c) is present simple; (d) is present perfect and changes the implied subject unnecessarily. Learning points: simple past interrogative uses “did”; passive “were/was + V3” → active “did + V1”; keep question word “Why” intact; “intimate” here means “inform/notify” (formal); choose the option that preserves tense and meaning.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

We were rearranging the library when the earthquake occurred.
options: The library was rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred.
The library were rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred.
When the earthquake occurred, we were rearranging the library.
The library was being rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred.
explanation: Past continuous (“were rearranging”) converts to passive as “was/were being + past participle”: “The library was being rearranged (by us) …”. Option (a) changes the tense to simple past; (b) is grammatically wrong (“library” is singular, so “was” not “were”); (c) remains active voice. Learning points: tense preservation is key in voice change; past continuous → was/were being + V3; object becomes subject; agent “by us” may be omitted if unnecessary; keep time clause (“when the earthquake occurred”) intact.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Are the scientists developing a new medicine for the disease?
options: Has a new medicine for the disease been developed by the scientists?
Is a new medicine for the disease being developed by the scientists?
Was a new medicine for the disease being developed by the scientists?
Is a new medicine for the disease developed by the scientists?
explanation: Present continuous interrogative (“Are … developing?”) converts to passive interrogative as “Is/Are + subject + being + V3 …?” → “Is a new medicine … being developed …?” Option (a) changes to present perfect; (c) changes to past; (d) becomes simple present and loses continuous sense. Learning points: are/is + V-ing → is/are + being + V3; keep question form by placing auxiliary before subject; “by the scientists” is the agent phrase; continuous emphasizes ongoing action; maintain meaning and tense while converting.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Where was the meeting held by the union leaders?
options: Where did the union leaders hold the meeting?
Where had the union leaders held the meeting?
Where have the union leaders held the meeting?
Where do the union leaders hold the meeting?
explanation: Passive simple past interrogative (“was held”) converts to active simple past interrogative using “did”: “Where did the union leaders hold the meeting?” Options (b) and (c) shift the tense to past perfect/present perfect; (d) shifts to simple present. Learning points: was/were + V3 (past passive) → did + subject + V1 (active question); keep “where” at the start; agent “by union leaders” becomes subject; ensure base verb after “did”; tense consistency is essential.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Had the final draft of the proposal been prepared by the secretary before the deadline?
options: Did the secretary prepare the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
Has the secretary prepared the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
Had the secretary prepared the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
Was the secretary preparing the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
explanation: Passive past perfect interrogative (“Had … been prepared”) converts to active past perfect interrogative: “Had the secretary prepared …?” Option (a) changes to simple past; (b) changes to present perfect; (d) changes to past continuous. Learning points: had + been + V3 (passive) → had + V3 (active); keep interrogative order (Had + subject + V3); agent becomes subject; time phrase “before the deadline” remains; past perfect indicates an action completed before another past reference time.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Will the committee approve the new policy tomorrow?
options: Has the new policy been approved by the committee tomorrow?
Will the new policy be approved by the committee tomorrow?
Will the new policy be approving by the committee tomorrow?
Was the new policy approved by the committee tomorrow?
explanation: In passive voice, the object (“the new policy”) becomes the subject, and the verb takes the form “will be + past participle”: “will be approved.” (a) changes tense to present perfect (“has been”), (c) is ungrammatical (“be approving”), and (d) changes tense to past (“was”). Learning points: (1) Future simple passive = will be + V3. (2) Keep time marker “tomorrow” unchanged. (3) Maintain modality (“will”) from the original. (4) Passive can omit the agent, but if included it uses “by.”

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Did the Romans defeat the Greeks?
options: Was the Greeks defeated by the Romans?
Did the Greeks defeated by the Romans?
Are the Greeks defeated by the Romans?
Were the Greeks defeated by the Romans?
explanation: Simple past interrogative active (“Did + subject + base verb”) changes to simple past interrogative passive (“Were/Was + object + past participle”). Since “the Greeks” is plural, we use “were”: “Were the Greeks defeated by the Romans?” (a) is wrong because it uses “was” with a plural subject. (b) is ungrammatical (uses “did” with a passive-like structure). (c) changes tense to present. Learning points: (1) Past passive: was/were + V3. (2) Interrogative passive keeps inversion (Were + subject...). (3) Ensure subject–verb agreement (Greeks → were). (4) Keep the agent with “by” if needed.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Were the examination papers being checked by the teachers until late at night?
options: Are the teachers checking the examination papers until late at night?
Were the teachers checking the examination papers until late at night?
Did the teachers check the examination papers until late at night?
Have the teachers checked the examination papers until late at night?
explanation: The passive sentence is in past continuous interrogative (“were being checked”). The corresponding active form is past continuous interrogative: “Were the teachers checking the examination papers until late at night?” (a) changes tense to present, (c) changes aspect to simple past, and (d) changes to present perfect. Learning points: (1) Past continuous passive = was/were being + V3. (2) Past continuous active = was/were + V-ing. (3) Keep interrogative inversion: Were + subject + V-ing. (4) Preserve time phrase “until late at night.”

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Couldn't the cancer be stopped from spreading further by the doctors?
options: Couldn't the doctors stop the cancer from spreading further?
Can't the doctors stop the cancer from spreading further?
Won't the doctors stop the cancer from spreading further?
Shouldn't the doctors stop the cancer from spreading further?
explanation: The passive uses a modal in past form (“couldn’t be stopped”). Active keeps the same modal and tense: “Couldn’t the doctors stop the cancer...?” (b) changes “couldn’t” to “can’t” (tense/meaning change), (c) changes modality to “won’t,” and (d) changes to “shouldn’t.” Learning points: (1) With modals, passive = modal + be + V3; active = modal + V1. (2) Keep the same modal to preserve meaning. (3) Agent “by the doctors” becomes the subject “the doctors.” (4) Maintain negation and interrogative structure.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The traffic department implements new traffic laws to reduce congestion.
options: New traffic laws were implemented by the traffic department to reduce congestion.
New traffic laws are being implemented by the traffic department to reduce congestion.
New traffic laws have been implemented by the traffic department to reduce congestion.
New traffic laws are implemented by the traffic department to reduce congestion.
explanation: The active sentence is in simple present (“implements”), so the most suitable passive is simple present passive: “are implemented.” (a) is simple past, (b) is present continuous, and (c) is present perfect—each changes the tense/aspect. Learning points: (1) Simple present passive = am/is/are + past participle. (2) Keep tense consistent when converting voice. (3) Agent (“by the traffic department”) is optional but acceptable. (4) Purpose phrase (“to reduce congestion”) remains unchanged.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Why did the baker add salt to the cake batter?
options: Why is salt added to the cake batter by the baker?
Why are salt added to the cake batter by the baker?
Why was salt added to the cake batter by the baker?
Why did salt added to the cake batter by the baker?
explanation: The active sentence is simple past interrogative (“did … add”), so passive should be simple past passive interrogative: “Why was salt added…?” (a) changes tense to present, (b) has subject–verb disagreement (“salt” is singular), and (d) is grammatically incorrect because “did” must be followed by the base verb and passive needs “be + past participle.” Learning points: (1) Past passive: was/were + V3. (2) In passive questions, invert “was/were” with the subject. (3) Ensure agreement: salt → was. (4) Don’t keep “did” in a passive construction.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Major breakthroughs in renewable energy have been achieved by scientists in recent decades.
options: Scientists achieve major breakthroughs in renewable energy in recent decades.
Scientists are achieving major breakthroughs in renewable energy in recent decades.
Scientists achieved major breakthroughs in renewable energy in recent decades.
Scientists have achieved major breakthroughs in renewable energy in recent decades.
explanation: The passive sentence uses present perfect (“have been achieved”), so active should also be present perfect: “Scientists have achieved…” Options (a), (b), and (c) change the tense/aspect and are therefore less suitable. Learning points: (1) Present perfect = have/has + V3. (2) Present perfect passive = have/has been + V3. (3) Maintain time expression compatibility (“in recent decades” fits present perfect). (4) Active voice places the doer (scientists) as the subject.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

By whom has this programme been authorised?
options: Who has authorised this programme?
Whom has authorised this programme?
This programme has been authorised by whom?
By who is this programme authorised?
explanation: The passive question asks for the agent (“by whom”), so in active voice the agent becomes the subject: “Who has authorised this programme?” (b) is wrong because “whom” is objective case, not subject. (c) keeps passive structure, and (d) changes tense to present simple/incorrect structure for the given meaning. Learning points: (1) Who = subject; whom = object. (2) “By whom” in passive typically becomes “who” in active. (3) Keep present perfect (“has authorised”). (4) Place the object (“this programme”) after the verb in active.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The engineers completed the structural analysis before the design phase began.
options: The structural analysis is completed by the engineers before the design phase began.
The structural analysis was being completed by the engineers before the design phase began.
The structural analysis had been completed by the engineers before the design phase began.
The structural analysis was completed by the engineers before the design phase began.
explanation: The sentence is in simple past (“completed”), so the suitable passive is simple past passive: “was completed”. Option (d) correctly uses “was completed” and keeps the agent (“by the engineers”). Option (a) shifts to present tense, (b) changes aspect to past continuous, and (c) changes to past perfect, which is not the most direct conversion here. Learning points: (1) Simple past active → was/were + V3. (2) Keep the object as the new subject (“structural analysis”). (3) Tense consistency matters across clauses. (4) “By + agent” is optional but used when needed. (5) Avoid unnecessary tense/aspect change in direct conversions.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The volunteers are cleaning the beach after the festival.
options: The beach is cleaned by the volunteers after the festival.
The beach is being cleaned by the volunteers after the festival.
The beach has been cleaned by the volunteers after the festival.
The beach will be cleaned by the volunteers after the festival.
explanation: The active sentence is present continuous (“are cleaning”), so the passive must be present continuous passive: “is/are being + V3” → “is being cleaned”. Option (b) matches tense and meaning. Option (a) becomes simple present, (c) becomes present perfect, and (d) becomes future. Learning points: (1) Present continuous passive form: am/is/are being + V3. (2) Subject–verb agreement: “beach” (singular) → “is”. (3) Keep time phrase (“after the festival”) intact. (4) Passive focuses on the action/receiver. (5) Don’t change tense unless required by meaning.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

New policies are being drafted by the government for immigrants.
options: The government drafts new policies for immigrants.
The government is drafting new policies for immigrants.
The government has been drafting new policies for immigrants.
The government drafted new policies for immigrants.
explanation: The passive is present continuous (“are being drafted”), so the active should also be present continuous: “The government is drafting new policies for immigrants.” Option (b) correctly converts the tense and places “the government” as subject. Learning points: (1) Passive: am/is/are being + V3 → Active: am/is/are + V-ing. (2) The object becomes subject in passive; reverse for active. (3) Maintain time/aspect. (4) “By + agent” becomes the subject in active. (5) Avoid tense shifts (simple present/past/perfect) unless the sentence demands it.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Several key policies have been introduced by the government to promote renewable energy.
options: The government has introduced several key policies to promote renewable energy.
The government introduces several key policies to promote renewable energy.
The government introduced several key policies to promote renewable energy.
The government is introducing several key policies to promote renewable energy.
explanation: The passive uses present perfect (“have been introduced”), so the active should be present perfect: “has introduced” (since “government” is singular). Option (a) is correct. Learning points: (1) Present perfect passive: have/has been + V3. (2) Active: have/has + V3. (3) Subject–verb agreement: government → has. (4) Keep the purpose clause (“to promote renewable energy”). (5) Present perfect signals relevance to present; don’t change to past/simple present.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Shakespeare wrote many plays.
options: Many plays were written by Shakespeare.
Many plays was written by Shakespeare.
Many plays have be written by Shakespeare.
Many plays has been written by Shakespeare.
explanation: Active: “Shakespeare wrote many plays.” (simple past). Passive uses “were written” (simple past passive) because the object “many plays” is plural. (b) has wrong subject–verb agreement (“plays” → “were”); (c) is grammatically incorrect (“have be”); (d) mixes tense/aspect and agreement (“plays” plural + “has”). Learning points: past simple passive = was/were + V3; choose “was” for singular, “were” for plural; keep agent with “by” when needed.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Do greenhouse gases cause global warming?
options: Is global warming caused by greenhouse gases?
Are global warming caused by greenhouse gases?
Does global warming caused by greenhouse gases?
Do global warming caused by greenhouse gases?
explanation: Present simple interrogative active → passive: “Is/Are + subject + past participle…?” Here “global warming” is singular, so “Is global warming caused by greenhouse gases?” is correct. (b) uses wrong verb (“Are” with singular “global warming”); (c) and (d) are ungrammatical because they retain “does/do” with a past participle structure incorrectly. Learning points: passive question structure often starts with auxiliary “is/are/was/were”; ensure subject–auxiliary agreement; keep the agent (“by greenhouse gases”) where relevant.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Will the project have been completed by the research team before the deadline?
options: Has the research team completed the project before the deadline?
Is the research team completing the project before the deadline?
Will the research team complete the project before the deadline?
Will the research team have completed the project before the deadline?
explanation: The given passive is future perfect (“will have been completed”). Active voice keeps the same tense: “Will the research team have completed the project before the deadline?” (d). (a) changes tense to present perfect; (b) changes to present continuous; (c) changes to simple future. Learning points: future perfect = will have + V3; passive future perfect = will have been + V3; in active, move the agent (“research team”) to subject position.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Why aren't benign tumours rejected by the body?
options: Why don't the body reject benign tumours?
Why won't the body reject benign tumours?
Why doesn't the body reject benign tumours?
Why can't the body reject benign tumours?
explanation: Passive present simple negative interrogative (“aren’t rejected”) converts to active present simple negative interrogative: “Why doesn’t the body reject benign tumours?” Option (c) is correct. (a) has wrong subject–auxiliary agreement (“the body” singular → “doesn’t,” not “don’t”); (b) changes meaning to future/volition; (d) changes meaning to inability. Learning points: match tense and polarity; check singular/plural agreement; avoid changing modality unless present in the original.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The teacher had praised the hardworking students.
options: The hardworking students had praised the teacher.
The hardworking students had been praised by the teacher.
The hardworking students were praised by the teacher.
The hardworking students have been praised by the teacher.
explanation: The verb tense is past perfect active (“had praised”), so passive must be past perfect passive: “had been praised.” Option (b) correctly makes “the hardworking students” the subject and uses “had been praised.” Option (a) stays active and changes meaning (reverses agent/patient). Option (c) is simple past passive, not past perfect. Option (d) is present perfect passive, wrong tense. Learning points: (1) Past perfect passive = had + been + V3. (2) Keep the original tense. (3) Object becomes subject in passive. (4) “by + agent” is optional but included here.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

How does he keep all these ancient clocks in working order?
options: How do all these ancient clocks kept in working order by him?
How are all these ancient clocks kept in working order by him?
How is all these ancient clocks kept in working order by him?
How are all these ancient clocks keep in working order by him?
explanation: Present simple active question → present simple passive question. Object “all these ancient clocks” is plural, so passive uses “are … kept.” Option (b) is grammatically correct. Option (a) is incorrect (missing auxiliary; wrong verb form “kept” placement). Option (c) uses “is” with plural subject. Option (d) uses base verb “keep” instead of past participle “kept.” Learning points: (1) Passive present simple: am/is/are + V3. (2) Plural subject → “are.” (3) Question word order: How + auxiliary + subject + V3. (4) Keep complements (“in working order”) unchanged.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Will the final decision be announced by the committee tomorrow afternoon?
options: Does the committee announce the final decision tomorrow afternoon?
Is the committee announcing the final decision tomorrow afternoon?
Has the committee announced the final decision tomorrow afternoon?
Will the committee announce the final decision tomorrow afternoon?
explanation: The passive is future simple (“will be announced”). Active must remain future simple: “Will the committee announce the final decision tomorrow afternoon?” Option (d) preserves tense and meaning. Options (a), (b), and (c) change tense (present simple/continuous/present perfect), so they are unsuitable. Learning points: (1) Future passive: will be + V3. (2) Future active: will + V1. (3) Passive agent (“by the committee”) becomes subject in active. (4) Time expressions remain in place.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Aren’t the packages inspected before dispatch?
options: Doesn’t someone inspect the packages before dispatch?
Don’t they inspected the packages before dispatch?
Aren’t they inspecting the packages before dispatch?
Can’t they inspect the packages before dispatch?
explanation: The passive is present simple (“are inspected”) in a negative question. Active present simple negative question can be: “Doesn’t someone inspect the packages before dispatch?” Option (a) matches tense and meaning (agent unspecified → “someone”). Option (b) is ungrammatical (“they inspected” after “don’t”). Option (c) changes tense to present continuous. Option (d) changes modality/meaning (“can’t” ≠ “aren’t”). Learning points: (1) Present simple passive ↔ present simple active. (2) When agent is unknown, use “someone/people/they” appropriately. (3) Don’t mix do-support with past tense verb. (4) Preserve modality and time reference.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Is the technician installing the security system in the building?
options: Has the security system been installed by the technician in the building?
Was the security system installed by the technician in the building?
Is the security system being installed by the technician in the building?
The security system is installed by the technician in the building.
explanation: The sentence is present continuous interrogative (“Is … installing …?”). Passive present continuous interrogative is “Is + object + being + past participle …?” Hence, (c) is correct. (a) is present perfect passive, (b) is past passive, and (d) is simple present passive (statement, not matching tense/aspect). Learning points: (1) Present continuous passive: am/is/are + being + V³. (2) Keep the question form (auxiliary before subject). (3) Match tense/aspect exactly; do not change time. (4) Object becomes subject in passive (“security system”). (5) Agent “by the technician” is optional but acceptable.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The street musician is playing a haunting tune on his flute.
options: A haunting tune is being played by the street musician.
A haunting tune is played by the street musician.
A haunting tune was being played by the street musician.
A haunting tune is playing by the street musician.
explanation: The sentence is present continuous (“is playing”), so passive must be present continuous passive: “is being played.” Therefore, (a) is correct. (b) changes to simple present, (c) changes to past continuous, and (d) is grammatically incorrect (“is playing by” is wrong). Learning points: (1) Active present continuous → passive: is/am/are being + V³. (2) Object (“a haunting tune”) becomes subject. (3) Keep tense consistent. (4) “By + agent” can be included when needed. (5) Avoid incorrect passive constructions like “is playing by.”

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Have the rules been explained by the supervisor?
options: Did the supervisor explain the rules?
Does the supervisor explain the rules?
Has the supervisor explained the rules?
Have the supervisor explained the rules?
explanation: The passive sentence is present perfect (“have been explained”) in interrogative form. Active present perfect interrogative uses “Has/Have + subject + V³ …?” With singular subject “the supervisor,” it becomes “Has the supervisor explained the rules?” Hence (c). (a) is past simple, (b) is simple present, and (d) is ungrammatical (“Have the supervisor…”). Learning points: (1) Present perfect passive: has/have been + V³. (2) Active present perfect: has/have + V³. (3) Singular subject → “has,” plural → “have.” (4) Keep question word order with auxiliary first. (5) Don’t change tense while converting voice.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Was the letter delivered by the postman yesterday evening?
options: Has the postman delivered the letter yesterday evening?
Did the postman deliver the letter yesterday evening?
Does the postman deliver the letter yesterday evening?
Was the postman delivering the letter yesterday evening?
explanation: The passive is simple past interrogative (“Was … delivered …?”). Active simple past interrogative is “Did + subject + base verb …?” → “Did the postman deliver the letter yesterday evening?” Hence (b). (a) changes tense to present perfect, (c) to simple present, (d) to past continuous. Learning points: (1) Simple past passive: was/were + V³. (2) Active interrogative in past: did + V¹. (3) Keep time marker (“yesterday evening”) consistent with past tense. (4) Do not use V³ after “did.” (5) Agent “by the postman” becomes subject “the postman.”

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

They will announce the results tomorrow.
options: The results are announced tomorrow.
The results will announced tomorrow.
The results will be announced tomorrow.
The results were announced tomorrow.
explanation: Future simple active “will announce” becomes passive “will be announced.” (a) changes tense to present; (b) is grammatically incorrect (missing “be”); (d) changes tense to past. Learning points: (1) will + V1 → will be + V3 in passive; (2) Object becomes subject (“results”); (3) Agent “by them” is usually omitted; (4) Keep time expression (“tomorrow”) unchanged; (5) Check tense consistency first.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Do water birds lay eggs in water or on land?
options: Are eggs laid by water birds in water or on land?
Do eggs laid by water birds in water or on land?
Did eggs laid by water birds in water or on land?
Is eggs laid by water birds in water or on land?
explanation: Present simple interrogative active (“Do + subject + V1”) converts to passive interrogative using “Are + object + V3 … by …?” → “Are eggs laid by water birds…?” Options (b), (c), (d) are ungrammatical or wrong tense/auxiliary. Learning points: (1) Do/does questions often become is/are/am in passive; (2) Choose singular/plural: eggs → are; (3) Past “did” would be “were”; (4) Keep prepositional phrase “in water or on land”; (5) Use “by + agent” when needed.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Was the speech delivered by the prime minister at the international summit?
options: Did the prime minister deliver the speech at the international summit?
Has the prime minister delivered the speech at the international summit?
Is the prime minister delivering the speech at the international summit?
Will the prime minister deliver the speech at the international summit?
explanation: The passive question uses “was delivered” (simple past), so the active form should be simple past interrogative: “Did + subject + V1” → “Did the prime minister deliver the speech…?” Other options change tense/aspect (present perfect/continuous/future). Learning points: (1) was/were + V3 → did + V1; (2) Passive agent becomes active subject; (3) Keep place phrase intact; (4) Maintain question form; (5) Check tense markers first.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

When were these pamphlets being distributed?
options: When were they distributing these pamphlets?
When are they distributing these pamphlets?
When will they distribute these pamphlets?
When were the distribution of pamphlets happening?
explanation: Passive past continuous interrogative “were being distributed” converts to active past continuous interrogative “were they distributing…?” (b) changes to present; (c) changes to future; (d) is awkward/incorrect noun-phrase construction. Learning points: (1) was/were being + V3 → was/were + V-ing; (2) Keep “when” at the start; (3) Add a reasonable subject (“they”) if not specified; (4) Keep tense/aspect same; (5) Avoid incorrect nominalisation (“were the distribution…”).

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The author published a children’s novella last year.
options: A children’s novella had been published by the author last year.
A children’s novella was published by the author last year.
A children’s novella is published by the author last year.
A children’s novella was being published by the author last year.
explanation: Simple past active (“published”) converts to simple past passive (“was/were + published”). So “A children’s novella was published by the author last year” is correct. “Had been published” is past perfect passive (changes tense), “is published” is present passive (wrong time), and “was being published” is past continuous passive (different aspect). Learning points: (1) Active: S + V2 + O → Passive: O + was/were + V3 (+ by + S); (2) keep tense/aspect unchanged; (3) time markers like “last year” signal simple past; (4) past perfect needs earlier-past reference; (5) continuous passive implies an ongoing action.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Why didn’t the critics like your new novel?
options: Why wasn’t your new novel liked by the critics?
Why isn’t your new novel liked by the critics?
Why didn’t your new novel liked by the critics?
Why wasn’t your new novel like by the critics?
explanation: In passive, object “your new novel” becomes subject; simple past negative question converts to “Why wasn’t + subject + V3 + by + agent?” Hence (a) is correct. (b) changes tense to present. (c) is ungrammatical (“didn’t” must be followed by base verb “like,” not “liked,” and passive is missing). (d) uses base verb “like” instead of past participle “liked.” Learning points: (1) passive needs V3 (“liked”); (2) keep tense: didn’t like → wasn’t liked; (3) question word “Why” stays at start; (4) agent can be kept with “by”; (5) watch auxiliary choice: was/were for past passive.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Several valuable discoveries have been made by scientists in the polar regions.
options: Scientists make several valuable discoveries in the polar regions.
Scientists are making several valuable discoveries in the polar regions.
Scientists have made several valuable discoveries in the polar regions.
Scientists made several valuable discoveries in the polar regions.
explanation: Present perfect passive “have been made” converts to present perfect active “have made.” So (c) is correct. (a) is simple present (tense shift), (b) is present continuous, and (d) is simple past. Learning points: (1) Present perfect passive: have/has been + V3; (2) Active: have/has + V3; (3) keep time-aspect when converting; (4) “several discoveries” stays as object in active; (5) “by scientists” becomes the subject “Scientists.”

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Which type of vehicles have been driven by you?
options: Which type of vehicles are you driven?
Which type of vehicles has you driven?
Which type of vehicles have you driven?
Which type of vehicles had you driven?
explanation: The passive present perfect “have been driven by you” converts to active present perfect “have you driven.” So (c) is correct. (a) is ungrammatical and changes meaning; (b) is incorrect auxiliary/word order; (d) shifts tense to past perfect. Learning points: (1) Question form in present perfect: have + subject + V3?; (2) passive agent “by you” becomes subject “you”; (3) keep “Which type of vehicles” as object/fronted wh-phrase; (4) maintain tense and number agreement; (5) avoid tense drift in conversions.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Does the management approve the new marketing strategy every quarter?
options: Is the new marketing strategy approved by the management every quarter?
Was the new marketing strategy approved by the management every quarter?
Has the new marketing strategy been approved by the management every quarter?
Is the new marketing strategy being approved by the management every quarter?
explanation: The active sentence is in simple present interrogative (“Does … approve?”). Its passive becomes simple present interrogative: “Is … approved by …?” Hence (a) is correct. (b) changes tense to past; (c) changes to present perfect; (d) changes to present continuous. Learning points: preserve tense and question form; object becomes subject; use “by” for agent when needed; auxiliary “do/does” disappears in passive.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Why do the villagers fear that man?
options: Why was that man feared by the villagers?
Why is the man feared by the villagers?
Why do this man feared by the villagers?
Why is that man feared by the villagers?
explanation: The active is simple present (“do … fear”). Passive must be simple present: “is feared”. Also the demonstrative “that man” should be retained as “that man” for closest match, making (d) best. (a) wrongly shifts to past; (c) is ungrammatical; (b) changes “that man” to “the man” (meaning shift). Learning points: keep tense; keep interrogative “why”; past participle with “be”; avoid changing determiners unnecessarily.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Will the task have been finished by the engineers before the deadline?
options: Do the engineers finish the task before the deadline?
Have the engineers finished the task before the deadline?
Will the engineers finish the task before the deadline?
Will the engineers have finished the task before the deadline?
explanation: The passive is in future perfect (“will have been finished”). The active must also be future perfect: “Will the engineers have finished the task before the deadline?” Hence (d). (a) is simple present; (b) is present perfect; (c) is simple future, all mismatching the tense/aspect. Learning points: match tense/aspect; passive “by + agent” becomes active subject; future perfect = will have + V3; keep time marker “before the deadline”.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

By whom will the new office be inaugurated?
options: Whom will inaugurate the new office?
Who will inaugurate the new office?
By who will inaugurate the new office?
By whom will inaugurate the new office?
explanation: The passive question asks about the agent (“By whom…”). In active voice, the agent becomes the subject: “Who will inaugurate the new office?” Thus (b) is correct. (a) is incorrect because “whom” cannot be the subject; (c) and (d) are ungrammatical. Learning points: “who” = subject; “whom” = object; passive “by whom” often converts to “who” in active; keep modal “will”.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

They are watching the movie carefully.
options: The movie was being watched carefully by them.
The movie is watched carefully by them.
The movie is being watched carefully by them.
The movie carefully is watched by them.
explanation: The sentence is in **present continuous** (“are watching”), so the passive form is **“is being watched”**. Therefore, “The movie is being watched carefully by them” is correct. (a) changes tense to past continuous, (b) changes aspect to simple present, and (d) has unnatural/incorrect word order. Learning points: (1) Present continuous passive: am/is/are + being + past participle, (2) object “the movie” becomes subject, (3) keep adverbs like “carefully” in a natural position, (4) “by them” is optional if agent is obvious/unimportant.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Did you notice the look on her face?
options: Was the look on her face noticed by you?
Did the look on her face noticed by you?
Did the look on her face notice by you?
Is the look on her face noticed by you?
explanation: The active sentence is in **simple past interrogative** (“Did you notice...?”). The passive interrogative uses **was/were + past participle**: “Was the look on her face noticed by you?” (b) and (c) are ungrammatical (wrong verb form/structure), and (d) wrongly changes tense to present. Learning points: (1) In passive questions, auxiliary comes before subject: “Was + subject + V3…?”, (2) “did” is not used with “V3” in passive formation, (3) maintain tense: did (past) → was/were (past), (4) “notice” past participle: noticed.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

The championship trophy will be presented by the governor at the closing ceremony.
options: The governor will present the championship trophy at the closing ceremony.
The governor presents the championship trophy at the closing ceremony.
The governor is presenting the championship trophy at the closing ceremony.
The governor has presented the championship trophy at the closing ceremony.
explanation: The passive sentence is in **simple future** (“will be presented”), so the active must be **will + base verb**: “will present.” Option (a) preserves tense and meaning. (b) changes to simple present, (c) to present continuous, and (d) to present perfect. Learning points: (1) Future passive: will be + V3, (2) Future active: will + V1, (3) agent “by the governor” becomes the subject, (4) keep place/time phrases (“at the closing ceremony”) unchanged.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Why is this day celebrated as 'Children's Day'?
options: Why did people celebrate this day as 'Children's Day'?
Why are they celebrating this day as 'Children's Day'?
Why do people celebrate this day as 'Children's Day'?
Why is 'Children's Day' celebrated as this day?
explanation: The passive is in **simple present** (“is celebrated”), so the active should also be **simple present**: “Why do people celebrate this day as ‘Children’s Day’?” (a) changes to past, (b) to present continuous, and (d) keeps passive and changes meaning/structure. Learning points: (1) Present passive: is/are + V3, (2) Present active question: do/does + subject + V1, (3) keep “why” questions aligned in tense, (4) “people” is a common generic subject when the agent is unspecified.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The archaeologists discovered ancient ruins during their excavation.
options: Ancient ruins were discovered by the archaeologists during their excavation.
Ancient ruins had been discovered by the archaeologists during their excavation.
Ancient ruins are discovered by the archaeologists during their excavation.
Ancient ruins are being discovered by the archaeologists during their excavation.
explanation: The active verb “discovered” is simple past, so the passive should be simple past: “were discovered.” Option (a) correctly changes object → subject (“ancient ruins”) and uses “were + past participle.” Option (b) is past perfect, changing tense incorrectly. Options (c) and (d) shift to present tenses, also incorrect. Learning points: keep tense unchanged in voice change; passive structure = be + V3; include agent (“by the archaeologists”) when needed.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Why did the board blacklist those players?
options: Why did those players blacklisted by the board?
Why are those players blacklisted by the board?
Why were those players blacklisted by the board?
Why were those players blacklist by the board?
explanation: The active is simple past interrogative (“did blacklist”), so the passive should be simple past interrogative: “Why were those players blacklisted by the board?” Option (c) uses “were” and past participle “blacklisted.” Option (a) is grammatically incorrect (missing auxiliary structure). Option (b) changes tense to present. Option (d) uses base verb “blacklist” instead of past participle. Learning points: in passive questions, move auxiliary before subject; ensure correct V3; keep tense and meaning intact.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

A new residential complex is being constructed by the government near the riverside.
options: The government constructs a new residential complex near the riverside.
The government is constructing a new residential complex near the riverside.
The government has constructed a new residential complex near the riverside.
The government constructed a new residential complex near the riverside.
explanation: The passive is present continuous (“is being constructed”), so the active should be present continuous: “The government is constructing…” Option (b) matches the tense and keeps meaning. Options (a), (c), and (d) change tense (simple present, present perfect, simple past). Learning points: identify auxiliary chain “is being”; active present continuous = is/are + V-ing; agent “by the government” becomes subject in active.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Why aren't the rules being followed by the players?
options: Why are the players not following the rules?
Why don't the players follow the rules?
Why didn't the players follow the rules?
Why aren't the players not following the rules?
explanation: The passive is present continuous negative interrogative (“aren’t being followed”), so the active should be present continuous negative interrogative: “Why are the players not following the rules?” Option (a) matches tense and meaning. Option (b) changes to simple present. Option (c) changes to simple past. Option (d) contains a wrong double negative (“aren’t… not”). Learning points: keep tense consistent; remove “being + V3” when converting to active; avoid double negatives unless intended.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Does the company provide customer support services 24/7?
options: Are customer support services provided by the company 24/7?
Is customer support service provided by the company 24/7?
Have customer support services been provided by the company 24/7?
Are customer support services being provided by the company 24/7?
explanation: The active sentence is simple present interrogative (“Does … provide …?”). The passive in simple present interrogative is “Are/Is + past participle …?” Hence, “Are customer support services provided by the company 24/7?” is correct (plural “services” → “are”). (b) mismatches number (“service” singular) compared to “services” given. (c) is present perfect passive, changing tense/aspect. (d) is present continuous passive, also changing aspect. Learning points: (1) does/do + V1 ↔ is/are + V3; (2) maintain tense/aspect; (3) match singular/plural with is/are; (4) keep question form by inversion; (5) retain meaning (general service availability).

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Why didn’t the police arrest the miscreants?
options: Why weren’t the miscreants arrested by the police?
Why wasn’t the miscreants arrested by the police?
Why didn’t the miscreants arrested by the police?
Why don’t the miscreants arrested by the police?
explanation: The active is simple past negative interrogative (“didn’t arrest”). Passive becomes “were/was + V3” in the past, with correct agreement: “miscreants” (plural) → “weren’t … arrested.” Thus (a) is correct. (b) has subject-verb disagreement (“wasn’t” with plural). (c) is ungrammatical (uses “didn’t” with V3 and wrong structure). (d) shifts tense to present (“don’t”), incorrect. Learning points: (1) did + not + V1 ↔ was/were + not + V3; (2) arrest → arrested (V3); (3) maintain past tense; (4) agreement: plural → were; (5) “why” questions keep “why” at the start.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

The evidence was being carefully examined by the investigating officers at that time.
options: The investigating officers examined the evidence carefully at that time.
The investigating officers were carefully examining the evidence at that time.
The investigating officers have carefully examined the evidence at that time.
The investigating officers examine the evidence carefully at that time.
explanation: The passive sentence is in past continuous (“was being examined”). The active equivalent should also be past continuous: “were examining.” Hence (b) is correct. (a) changes tense to simple past. (c) changes to present perfect. (d) changes to simple present. Learning points: (1) was/were being + V3 ↔ was/were + V-ing; (2) keep time marker “at that time” (often continuous); (3) keep adverbs (“carefully”) near the verb; (4) subject in active = agent (“investigating officers”); (5) passive-to-active often reduces wordiness.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Which type of books are read by you?
options: Which type of books did you read?
Which type of books do you read?
Which type of books are you read?
Which type of books have you read?
explanation: The passive is simple present (“are read”) with an interrogative form. The active simple present interrogative becomes “do you read.” Therefore, (b) is correct. (a) changes tense to past. (c) is ungrammatical. (d) changes aspect to present perfect. Learning points: (1) are/is + V3 (passive present) ↔ do/does + V1 (active present); (2) “by you” becomes subject “you”; (3) maintain tense; (4) in questions, use auxiliary “do/does”; (5) ensure correct subject-verb agreement: “you read,” not “you reads.”

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

They say she writes beautiful poems.
options: It is said that she writes beautiful poems.
She is say to write beautiful poems.
It says she writes beautiful poems.
She said to writes beautiful poems.
explanation: The correct impersonal passive reporting form is “It is said that + clause.” Option (b) is ungrammatical (“is say”); (c) is incorrect reporting structure; (d) is ungrammatical and tense-confused. Learning points: (1) Reporting passive: It is said/believed/thought that…. (2) Use past participle: said. (3) Keep tense of the reported clause appropriate. (4) Avoid wrong infinitive/verb forms.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Does she check all the final calculations before the launch?
options: Are all the final calculations checked by her before the launch?
Is all the final calculations checked by her before the launch?
Will all the final calculations be checked by her before the launch?
Does all the final calculations checked by her before the launch?
explanation: Present simple interrogative passive uses “Are/Is + subject + past participle…?” With plural “calculations”, the auxiliary must be “are”. (b) has subject–verb disagreement; (c) changes tense to future; (d) is structurally wrong. Learning points: (1) Passive question pattern: auxiliary + subject + V3. (2) Match auxiliary to number (is/are). (3) Preserve tense/aspect while converting. (4) Agent “by her” is optional but correct.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

The new rules had been strictly enforced by the government before the elections.
options: The government enforces the new rules strictly before the elections.
The government enforced the new rules strictly before the elections.
The government had strictly enforced the new rules before the elections.
The government is strictly enforcing the new rules before the elections.
explanation: “Had been enforced” is past perfect passive; the active must be past perfect: “had enforced”. Options (a), (b), and (d) change tense/aspect. Learning points: (1) Past perfect passive = had been + V3. (2) Past perfect active = had + V3/V2 (past participle). (3) Keep time marker “before…” consistent. (4) Maintain adverb placement (“strictly”) naturally.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

How is so much stress handled by her?
options: How does she handle so much stress?
How do she handle so much stress?
How did she handle so much stress?
How will she handle so much stress?
explanation: The passive is present simple (“is handled”); the active must be present simple interrogative: “does + subject + base verb”. Option (b) has wrong auxiliary with “she”; (c) changes to past; (d) changes to future. Learning points: (1) Present simple question: does/do + base verb. (2) “She” takes “does”. (3) Preserve tense in voice conversion. (4) Passive agent becomes active subject.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?

Didn't you keep the heavy box in the attic?
options: Wasn't the heavy box kept in the attic by you?
Didn't the heavy box kept in the attic by you?
Weren't the heavy box kept in the attic by you?
Wasn't the heavy box keep in the attic by you?
explanation:
The active interrogative in simple past (“Didn’t you keep…?”) becomes passive as “Wasn’t the heavy box kept… (by you)?” using “was + past participle (kept).”

Why other options are wrong: (b) is grammatically incorrect (missing auxiliary and wrong verb form); (c) has subject-verb disagreement (“box” is singular → wasn’t); (d) uses wrong verb form (“keep” instead of “kept”).

Learning points: (1) Simple past passive: was/were + V3. (2) Singular subject → was. (3) “Did” questions convert to “was/were” in passive. (4) Keep → kept (V3). (5) “by you” can be optional if agent is obvious.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Someone has broken into our warehouse.
options: Our warehouse has been broke into by someone.
Our warehouse has been broked into.
Our warehouse has been broken into.
Our warehouse has been broken by someone.
explanation:
Present perfect active (“has broken into”) becomes present perfect passive: “has been broken into.” Option (c) is correct and idiomatic.

Why other options are wrong: (a) uses wrong past participle “broke”; (b) uses incorrect form “broked”; (d) changes meaning (“broken by someone” doesn’t carry “break into” = enter illegally).

Learning points: (1) Present perfect passive = has/have been + V3. (2) Phrasal verb “break into” must stay intact. (3) Use correct V3: broken. (4) Passive may omit agent if unknown. (5) Meaning must remain the same.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Won't you share the prize money with your siblings?
options: Will the prize money be shared by you with your siblings?
Won't the prize money be share by you with your siblings?
Won't the prize money shared by you with your siblings?
Won't the prize money be shared by you with your siblings?
explanation:
The correct passive keeps the modal form: “won’t … be + V3” → “Won’t the prize money be shared by you…?”

Why other options are wrong: (a) changes the auxiliary/modal structure; (b) uses wrong verb form “be share”; (c) misses “be.”

Learning points: (1) Modal passive: modal + be + V3. (2) Keep question form and negativity (“won’t”). (3) Past participle of share = shared. (4) Don’t omit “be” in passive. (5) Preserve original meaning and tone.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

You are requested not to enter.
options: Please do not enter.
Do not enter.
Please not to enter.
Your entry is not requested.
explanation:
The passive “You are requested not to enter” becomes an active polite instruction: “Please do not enter.” Option (a) best retains the sense of a request.

Why other options are wrong: (b) is a command and loses the request/politeness nuance; (c) is grammatically incorrect; (d) is awkward and not a natural active-voice equivalent.

Learning points: (1) Passive requests often convert to polite imperatives. (2) “Please do not …” conveys request. (3) Avoid ungrammatical “Please not to …”. (4) Naturalness matters in transformation questions. (5) Preserve meaning (request vs order).

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

The police arrested the thief last night.
options: The police was arrested the thief last night.
The thief is arrested last night by the police.
The thief was arrested by the police last night.
The thief has been arrested last night.
explanation:
Simple past active (“arrested”) converts to simple past passive (“was/were + past participle”): “The thief was arrested by the police last night.”

Why other options are wrong: (a) wrong structure; (b) tense mismatch (“is” with “last night”); (d) present perfect (“has been”) doesn’t fit “last night.”

Learning points: (1) Past simple → was/were + V3. (2) Object becomes subject in passive. (3) Keep time markers consistent with tense. (4) “By + agent” is optional but correct here. (5) Avoid tense shifts in voice conversion.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?**

Will she forgive him after all this time?
options: Will he forgive by her after all this time?
Will he be forgiven by her after all this time?
Will he be forgive by her after all this time?
Will he forgiven by her after all this time?
explanation:
Future simple interrogative passive is “Will + subject + be + past participle”: “Will he be forgiven by her after all this time?”

Why other options are wrong: (a) missing “be” and wrong verb form; (c) uses base form “forgive” instead of past participle “forgiven”; (d) missing “be.”

Learning points: (1) Passive needs “be” form. (2) Use V3 (past participle) in passive. (3) Keep question order with auxiliary “will” at start. (4) Subject-object swap: she↔him. (5) Check verb forms: forgive–forgave–forgiven.

question:
**Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?**

Let the vote of thanks be given by him.
options: He will give the vote of thanks.
Let him give the vote of thanks.
The vote of thanks will be given by him.
He may give the vote of thanks.
explanation:
The passive structure with “Let + object + be + V3” converts to active as “Let + agent + V1”: “Let him give the vote of thanks.”

Why other options are wrong: (a) changes mood to future statement; (c) remains passive; (d) changes meaning by adding modality (“may”).

Learning points: (1) “Let + object + be + V3” is a passive imperative. (2) Active imperative: “Let + doer + V1.” (3) Preserve the command/request tone. (4) Avoid adding/modifying tense or modality. (5) Ensure agent (“him”) becomes the doer in active.
